What about systemd? Is it involved in this dump?

Systemd has gathered a lot of criticism. Very few people like it compared to what it replaced, init.d, which is a more classic init system. As a brief explanation, especially as I'm not an expert on it, init is the program that runs right after the kernel has completely prepared the system for use, and it takes over the boot process and remains as the ultimate root process for (theoretically) the entire uptime of the system. There have been a few init systems for Linux and Unix, but most of them have been based on tried-and-true principles, often managing a large number of scripts that oversee system startup, starting up and linking various problems that allow the system to be ready to use. For instance, if your system was a web server, it might have extensive support for Apache startup in the scripts.

Systemd, however, has been introduced over the last 3-4 years, and it has rapidly replaced init.d on the vast majority of the major distributions, particularly the two most influential distros, Red Hat and Debian. This means that, since a very large number of distributions (including, but far from limited to, all flavors of Ubuntu, Mint, SuSE... truth be told, most of the well known ones other than Gentoo and Slackware) are built on one of these two, systemd exclusivity puts distro developers in a very nasty position wherein they either accept systemd or they have to continually rewrite upstream contributions, which will only increase in quantity and difficulty over time. However, despite this widespread acceptance, this does not mean that people like it. In a perverse way, it is not entirely unlike Windows 10 in some respects. Its design is poor (one single program where there were many; the many were to enhance modularity and customizability, and to contain faults and security problems, among other things). It is generally binary only whereas much of what came before was script-based, making it very easy to modify on the fly. Most old-school system administrators, and many newer ones, believe that it's at best an attempt to fix what isn't broken, and breaks a lot of things in the process, directly and indirectly. The development team is known for being rude and forcing people to capitulate to it rather than being a good software citizen and trying to work with the ecosystem, and the head developer, Pottering, is especially known for acting like an ass (and not in the way Linus Torvalds does, which is more productive).

Nobody really knows quite why it's become so pervasive, so quickly; it seems like Red Hat installed it and suddenly Debian picked it up, and since most distros use those as their base, they have a lot of work to do to get away from them. An increasing number of packages are requiring systemd, including Gnome, which should have nothing whatsoever to do with systemd. In some cases this seems to be against the will of the developers (who had their initial work broken by systemd's changes), but they don't necessarily have the resources to develop for both systemd and more conventional init.d systems. It is suffering from considerable scope creep as well, reaching into areas that its predecessor never touched (and for good reason). This means that it is competing against projects that specialize in more specific programs that were useful under init.d, and as such it is eliminating a specialized program that can do more. While this might just be the market, one might say, the fact is that systemd is not a specialist and likely cannot match the specialized teams which concentrate in their specific domain and relied on init.d to string it all together. This is in gross violation of the Unix design philosophy, which has most basic and critical system utilities in single-purpose tools that are extremely good at what they do but usually specialized, and strung together at a higher level by more general scripts and/or programs. Speaking of which, it also lessens the Unix compatibility that Linux has, because init.d is derived greatly from Unix in spirit if not literal code, while systemd is generally Linux-only. systemd itself is not exactly all that great as software, either. Programming is often seen as poor and buggy; I wish I had a particular article I read a few days ago in front of me, but it had a lot of cases it linked to showing how they have broken promises (and with it broken compatibility, leaving some developers high and dry), left in bugs and in many cases just guessed at things that the program should guard against or try to detect rather than assume. It has been compared to Windows' svchost, specifically that it takes most of its weaknesses and ports them to Linux.

People have been concerned as to why this is for many reasons. Some believe that Red Hat was in collusion with Microsoft, who was trying to use this to control and possibly weaken Linux, which is especially concerning since they arguably have a large investment in it while going to being a cloud provider. Others have thought that Red Hat was attempting to leverage their control to gain a stranglehold over Linux in a rather draconian way, particularly leveraging their hold on the Gnome project (and the fact that Gnome is the most popular desktop system for Linux at the moment - if they can make Gnome need it, then they can further strengthen their hand in trying to force it on other distros). Others have thought the government may have had something to do with it. Even if it's unintentional, systemd, being a nice big fat monolithic target, probably has plenty of bugs in it that would allow for root-level access, and it's a fair bet that a lot of people - legitimate developers, intelligence agencies and hackers alike - have been looking to find them, and in the latter two cases, exploit them.

This is all off the top of my head so I could be wrong, but those are the general parts. I would invite anyone who knows this topic better than I do to contribute and possibly correct me if I'm getting anything grossly wrong. I do not know if it is directly involved in this dump, but the suspicion is, suffice it to say, warranted, that it may be in future dumps.
